# ✈️ The Ultimate Guide to the Flight 100ml Liquids Rule (2026 Edition)

![Liquids Flight Guide Header](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Packing for a flight can be a stressful balancing act. Between weight limits, baggage fees, and security regulations, there is one rule that consistently trips up even the most seasoned travelers: **the 100ml liquids rule** [4]. 

We have all been there—standing in the security line, watching a beloved bottle of perfume, high-end face cream, or even a jar of peanut butter get swept into the bin by an airport security officer. 

But why does this rule exist? What actually counts as a "liquid"? And how are new security technologies in 2026 changing the way we pack? This comprehensive guide breaks down everything you need to know to breeze through airport security without losing your toiletries.

---

## 1. 🛡️ Why Does the 100ml Rule Exist?

The restriction on carry-on liquids is not a random rule designed to make you purchase overpriced airport water. It has its roots in global security history. 

In August 2006, British police thwarted a major terrorist plot to detonate liquid explosives disguised as soft drinks aboard transatlantic flights. The plan involved assembling explosives mid-flight using common household chemicals. 

In response, aviation authorities worldwide took immediate action. Initially, all liquids were banned from cabin baggage entirely. Within a few months, security agencies like the TSA (Transportation Security Administration) and EU security bodies established a compromise based on extensive laboratory testing: **the 100ml (3.4 ounces) limit**. 

Scientists determined that liquid explosives in volumes under 100ml could not be easily combined to create a blast of critical mass. This compromise allowed passengers to bring essential toiletries while maintaining a secure cabin environment. It has remained the global aviation standard ever since.

---

## 2. 🧴 What Actually Counts as a "Liquid"? (The LAGs Definition)

Most travelers know that water, shampoo, and mouthwash are liquids. However, airport security operates under a much broader classification known as **LAGs: Liquids, Aerosols, and Gels** [4]. 

If an item can be poured, squeezed, sprayed, smeared, or spread, security officers will classify it as a liquid. If it does not hold its shape outside of its container, it must fit under the 100ml rule.

Here are some of the most common, surprising, and frequently confiscated items that people get wrong:

*   **🥪 Spreads and Foods:** Peanut butter, Nutella, hummus, honey, maple syrup, jam, cream cheese, and wet pet food are all classified as liquids [1]. Even a soft, creamy cheese like Brie can be confiscated if it exceeds 100ml.
*   **💄 Cosmetics and Toiletries:** Mascara, liquid foundation, lip gloss, toothpaste, creams, lotions, hair gel, and roll-on deodorants are all LAGs [1, 4]. 
*   **🌸 Aerosols:** Hairspray, spray deodorants, shaving cream, and dry shampoo fall strictly under the liquids umbrella [1, 4].
*   **❄️ Gelled items:** Gel shoe inserts, gel-filled cooling packs, and snowglobes are also restricted.

> 💡 **The Golden Rule of Packing:** If you can smear it, spray it, or squeeze it, pack it as a liquid. When in doubt, check your items in our [liquids search tool](https://canitakethis.co/plane/liquids/) before you head to the airport [4].

---

## 3. 👜 The 3-1-1 / 1-Liter Bag Rule Explained

To bring liquids in your carry-on, you must follow the three core rules of liquid geometry (often called the **3-1-1 rule** by the TSA):

1.  **🧴 3.4 Ounces (100ml) or Less:** All liquid containers must have a maximum capacity of 100ml or less.
2.  **👝 1 Clear Plastic Bag:** All containers must fit comfortably inside a single, transparent, resealable plastic bag. The bag’s volume must not exceed **1 liter** (roughly 1 quart), and its dimensions should be approximately 20cm x 20cm (8 x 8 inches).
3.  **🚶 1 Bag Per Passenger:** Each traveler is allowed only one liquids bag. It must be pulled out of your hand luggage and placed in a separate tray at the security scanner.

![1-Liter Bag Diagram](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

### 🛑 The "Container Capacity" Trap
The most common mistake travelers make is bringing a large bottle that is only partially full. **Security measures the container's capacity, not the liquid inside.** 
*   A 200ml bottle containing only 20ml of shampoo **will be confiscated**.
*   You must decant your liquids into designated travel-sized bottles (100ml or under) before your trip.

---

## 4. ✨ Crucial Exceptions to the Rule

Thankfully, global aviation security agencies recognize that some liquids are essential. There are three major exemptions to the strict 100ml limit:

### A. 🍼 Baby Milk, Formula, and Food
If you are traveling with an infant (typically aged 2 or under), you are permitted to bring breast milk, formula, sterilized water, baby juice, and baby food jars in quantities larger than 100ml.
*   These items do not need to fit inside your 1-liter plastic bag.
*   You must declare them to airport security officers for separate screening.
*   The baby must be traveling with you for the exemption to apply (though some jurisdictions, like the US, allow breast milk to be carried without the baby present).

### B. 💊 Prescription Medications and Medical Liquids
Essential liquid, gel, or aerosol medications are fully exempt from the 100ml rule [1, 4]. This includes insulin, saline solution for contact lenses, inhalers, and liquid cough medicines.
*   You can carry them in the quantities required for your trip.
*   They should be kept separate from your toiletries bag and declared at security.
*   **Pro Tip:** To prevent delays, keep your medications in their original packaging with the pharmacy label matching your boarding pass, or carry a doctor’s note explaining your medical necessity.

### C. 🛍️ Duty-Free Liquids
Liquids purchased at duty-free shops after the security checkpoint are exempt from carry-on limits, even on connecting flights, provided they are packed in a **Secure Tamper-Evident Bag (STEB)**.
*   The store clerk will seal your alcohol, perfume, or cosmetics in a clear bag with a red border [1, 4].
*   **Do not open this bag** until you reach your final destination. If you have a layover and must pass through security again, the bag must remain sealed with the purchase receipt visible inside.

---

## 5. 🚀 The 2026 Landscape: How New Airport Scanners are Changing the Rules

If you have traveled recently, you might have noticed some airports no longer require you to remove liquids from your bags. This is thanks to the rollout of advanced **Computed Tomography (CT) / C3 security scanners**.

These next-generation scanners use 3D X-ray imaging and powerful algorithms to analyze the molecular structure of items inside your bag. They can instantly distinguish between safe liquids and potentially explosive chemicals.

### ⚠️ The Big Catch: A Two-Speed Travel World
While some major global hubs (such as London Heathrow, Amsterdam Schiphol, and selected terminals in the US and Europe) have lifted the 100ml limit or allowed liquids to stay in bags, **the rollout is highly inconsistent**. 
*   Many airports still operate older 2D scanners and strictly enforce the 1-liter bag rule.
*   Even if your departure airport has upgraded scanners, your **return airport or connecting hub** might not.
*   To avoid having your expensive items confiscated on your return journey, **always pack under the 100ml rule** unless you are absolutely certain both ends of your trip support the new scanners.

When planning your journey, remember that individual airlines can sometimes enforce their own unique cabin constraints, which affects how you pack your liquids bag. For instance, if you are flying on a budget carrier with strict hand luggage dimensions, your toiletries bag will need to fit tightly alongside your other essentials.

## 7. ❓ Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

### Q: Do wet wipes and makeup remover wipes count as liquids?
No. Wet wipes, baby wipes, and makeup remover wipes are classified as solid items. They do not need to go into your 1-liter liquids bag.

### Q: Does solid bar soap or solid deodorant count as a liquid?
No. Solid toiletries, such as bar soap, solid stick deodorant, solid perfume, and lipstick, are considered solids and are exempt from the liquids bag. Gel or roll-on deodorants, however, must go in the bag.

### Q: Can I bring contact lens solution?
Yes. Contact lens solution is classified as an over-the-counter medical liquid. It is exempt from the 100ml limit, but you must declare it to security officers for separate screening. Many travelers still prefer to pack travel-sized bottles (under 100ml) in their standard liquids bag to save time.

### Q: What happens if my liquids bag won't fully zip close?
If your 1-liter bag cannot be sealed completely, security officers may ask you to discard some items until it zips easily. Always leave a little breathing room in your bag when packing.
